summary: This informational document describes a URN namespace for naming persistent resources defined by Aerospace and Defence Industries Association of Europe Specification 1000D.

plainLanguage.summary: Things in a big aircraft manual need names that never change, like permanent library call numbers. This sets up the naming scheme used for that manual standard.

questions: how are aerospace documentation resources named
subtitle: Permanent, location-independent names for aerospace and defense technical documentation resources.

tldr.problem: Aerospace and defense organizations use S1000D, an international specification for technical publications (aircraft manuals, maintenance documentation). Resources created under this standard need permanent identifiers that do not depend on where they are stored, so they can be found in web systems and remain stable across reorganizations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a URN namespace for S1000D resources using a structured identifier scheme. URNs are location-independent names (like ISBN numbers), as opposed to URLs which are location-dependent. The S1000D namespace uses prefixes for different resource types (DMC, PMC, CSN, ICN, COM, DDN, DML) followed by a code string, with optional issue and language tags.
tldr.outcome: Aerospace and defense companies can assign permanent, globally unique names to their S1000D-compliant technical resources, enabling better resource management systems and stable references.

facts.label: Resource type prefixes
facts.value: 7 (DMC, PMC, CSN, ICN, COM, DDN, DML)

today: RFC 4688 is an Informational document from October 2006 and has not been updated or obsoleted. It remains the active definition of the S1000D URN namespace, registered with IANA. Aerospace and defense organizations continue to use S1000D and its URN namespace for technical documentation management.

sections.title: S1000D and Its Naming Challenge
sections.content:
S1000D (Specification 1000D) is an international standard for creating technical documentation, especially aircraft and aerospace maintenance manuals. It was developed jointly by the Aerospace and Defence Industries Association of Europe (ASD) and the Aerospace Industries Association of America (AIA).

The specification uses ISO and W3C standards and focuses on modular, reusable documentation components. A single aircraft manual might contain thousands of separate information modules—engine specifications, wiring diagrams, maintenance procedures—that can be assembled in different ways and reused across projects.

The challenge is naming these resources so they can be uniquely identified and found anywhere, whether they are stored on a web server, in a company database, or shared across organizations. A regular web URL would break if the file moved; an ISBN-like identifier would stay the same forever. This RFC creates such an identifier scheme using URNs.
sections.plainLanguage: Aircraft manuals are huge and divided into thousands of pieces—engine info, wiring diagrams, procedures. These pieces get reused. We need names for them that work the same way ISBN numbers work for books: they never change, no matter where the book sits on the shelf.

sections.title: URNs and Namespaces
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Name (URN) is a persistent identifier for a resource. Unlike a URL (which tells you where something is), a URN identifies what something is. An ISBN like 978-0-486-27557-8 is a URN for a book. It is location-independent: you can find that book at a library, a bookstore, or online; the ISBN stays the same.

URNs are organized into namespaces. The ISBN namespace holds book identifiers. The DOI namespace holds digital object identifiers. The S1000D namespace (defined by this RFC) holds identifiers for S1000D resources.

A URN has the format URN:namespace:namespace-specific-string. For S1000D, the format is URN:S1000D:resourcecode, where the resource code has a defined structure.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN is like a library catalog number: it says what something is, not where it is. The S1000D namespace is a special set of library numbers just for aerospace manuals.

sections.title: The S1000D Resource Code Structure
sections.content:
Every S1000D URN has a resource type prefix, a resource code string, and optional issue and language tags.

The resource type prefixes are:

  • DMC (Data Module Code): an information module like a procedure or specification.
  • PMC (Publication Module Code): a publication (a published document or manual).
  • CSN (Catalogue Sequence Number): an entry in a catalog or index.
  • ICN (Illustration Control Number): a diagram or illustration.
  • COM (Comment Code): a comment or annotation on a resource.
  • DDN (Data Dispatch Notice): a notice of changed or new resources.
  • DML (Data Module List): a list grouping related modules.

The code string follows the syntax defined in the S1000D specification itself and includes dashes and alphanumeric characters (e.g., AE-A-07-05-0000-00A-040A-A).

Optional issue and language tags are appended with underscores: _I-001 means issue 001, and _L-EN means English. An example complete URN: URN:S1000D:DMC-AE-A-07-05-0000-00A-040A-A_I-001_L-EN.
sections.plainLanguage: Every resource has a type ("this is a procedure" or "this is a diagram"), then a code (like a catalog number), then optionally which version and language ("issue 5, in Spanish").

sections.title: Ensuring Global Uniqueness
sections.content:
S1000D ensures that all URNs are globally unique through a registration process. Each organization or project that creates S1000D resources is assigned a Model Identifier by the NATO Maintenance and Supply Agency (NAMSA). This Model Identifier is never reused.

All resource codes created by that project are prefixed with the project's Model Identifier, making every code globally unique within that project space. Since the Model Identifier itself is globally unique and unreused, the combination is unique worldwide.

This design means that if two different aerospace companies both create a data module with the same local code, the two URNs are still different because each company's codes begin with its unique Model Identifier.

Once a resource is published and assigned a URN, the identifier persists forever. This allows organizations to reference resources across projects and time, knowing the name will never change.
sections.plainLanguage: Every company gets a unique prefix ("Airbus gets AB, Boeing gets BX"). All their manuals start with that prefix. So two companies can both make a "procedure 001," but they get different URNs because of the prefix.
